# Block 5: Instructions and skills {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
source("R/skill_download.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

The previous block showed that the further up the autonomy ladder an assistant
works, the more its unstated assumptions land in your files. This block is how
you state your conventions once, so you do not repeat them in every prompt.

There are two mechanisms, distinguished by when they load:

- **Instructions** live in an `r glossary("instruction file")` that loads into
  every conversation automatically. Use it for what is always true of the
  project: structure, style, reproducibility rules.
- **Skills** load only when invoked by name or judged relevant from their
  description. A `r glossary("skill")` suits a procedure you need sometimes:
  producing a publication figure, cleaning data against a codebook, reviewing
  code.

Both are requests. The model usually follows them, but nothing guarantees it.
Rules that must hold every time belong in the enforced controls of
[Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd).

*⏱ ~45 minutes*


## Part A: Instructions

### Where Claude Code looks

| File | Claude Code | Posit Assistant |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` (repository root) | Via an import in `CLAUDE.md` | Read as project memory |
| `CLAUDE.md` | Read at the start of every conversation | — |

This course uses **one source of truth**: conventions live in `AGENTS.md`, and
`CLAUDE.md` contains a single line that imports it:

```text
@AGENTS.md
```

Other tools read `AGENTS.md` too (see *Going further*), so one file serves them
all. Skills, in Part B, follow the same idea: one master copy, read by each
tool from where it looks.

### Writing instructions that work

- **One instruction per line.** Short, concrete statements are easier to check
  than paragraphs, for the model and for you.
- **Describe what you actually do.** An instruction your existing code breaks
  sends the model mixed signals. The test is whether your own scripts obey it.
- **Be specific.** "Use the native pipe `|>`" can be checked; "write clean,
  idiomatic code" cannot.
- **Keep it short.** The file loads into every request. Anthropic advises
  keeping Claude Code's always-loaded file under about 200 lines; aim far
  lower.
- **Add a rule when a mistake repeats.** If the assistant gets the same
  convention wrong twice, that convention belongs in the file. A one-off
  correction in chat is forgotten in the next conversation.
- **Do not put guarantees here.** "Never edit raw data" is worth stating, but
  enforce it with the controls in [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd).


### Activity: Build and test your AGENTS.md

You start from a provided draft rather than a blank page. Your job is to make
it describe *your* practice, then prove that Claude Code reads it.

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Adapt, connect, verify (15 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Start:** your workshop repository on `main`, committed and clean, with no
`AGENTS.md` yet. Check the agent's work from the R console and Git pane, as in
[checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work).

**1. Baseline.** With no `AGENTS.md` present, start Claude Code in `plan` mode
in the project's Terminal tab.

**In the terminal:**

```bash
claude --permission-mode plan
```

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot of
mass_post_g by treatment arm. Show the R code in your reply; do not create
any files.
```

Keep the answer. Asking for the code in the reply matters: in `plan` mode it
may otherwise describe a plan with no code, and the canary in step 5 would have
nowhere to appear.

**2. Copy the starting draft.** In the R console,
`usethis::edit_file("AGENTS.md")` creates `AGENTS.md` in the repository root
and opens it. Paste in the draft below. It includes a `r glossary("canary")`: a
fixed first line the assistant is asked to put in any R code it writes, so you
can see whether the file was loaded. The "Tests" rules ask the agent to prove
its own work after every edit, which later blocks rely on.

```markdown
# Project conventions: voles analysis

## Canary
When you write or edit R code, make the first line of the first code block:
# agents-md: active v1

## Structure
- Raw data live in data/raw/ and are never modified.
- Derived data go to data/derived/; figures and tables go to outputs/.
- Reusable functions live in scripts/functions/.

## R style
- Tidyverse style, native pipe |>, snake_case names, <- for assignment.
- Write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F.
- Build every path with here::here() (or here() after library(here)). Never
  use setwd() or rm(list = ls()).
- Read CSV files with readr and explicit col_types.

## Reproducibility
- Packages are managed with renv. Do not call install.packages(); ask before
  adding a package.
- Do not edit renv.lock.
- Set a seed immediately before any random step.
- Every script must run in a fresh R session.
- Every script must run with Rscript from the project root; after writing one,
  run it that way and report the exit status.
- Save figures with ggsave() to outputs/.

## Tests
- After editing any R file, run Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')" and
  paste the final summary line verbatim.
- Never edit anything in tests/fixtures/, an existing expectation or a
  tolerance to make a test pass.
- Every new function in scripts/functions/ gets a test with at least one
  known-answer case on a small tibble, including an NA; expected values are
  worked out by hand, never by running the code under test.

## Data integrity
- Never drop rows silently; state the reason for every filter in a comment.
- Report the number of observations behind every summary statistic.

## Statistics
- Label each analysis as exploratory or confirmatory.
- Never type numerical results into text; compute them in code.

## Working with me
- Before changing more than one file, present a plan and wait for approval.
- Do not edit anything under data/raw/, tests/fixtures/ or .github/.
```

**3. Make it yours.** Delete any rule you do not actually follow. Then add one
style convention you genuinely follow that the draft does not state, and one
reproducibility or statistical convention you always apply. Keep the canary
line. Later blocks rely on the "Tests", "Statistics" and "Working with me" rules,
so keep those too.

**4. Connect Claude Code.** Create `CLAUDE.md` in the repository root
containing only the line `@AGENTS.md`. In the R console:

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
writeLines("@AGENTS.md", here::here("CLAUDE.md"))
testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_controls.R"))
```

The test confirms that `CLAUDE.md` holds exactly that one line and that the
shipped deny rules are all still in place.

**5. Verify.** Commit from the Git pane. Then leave Claude Code (`/exit`) and
start it again in the Terminal tab, so it loads the new files at the start of
the conversation, and repeat the step 1 prompt.

- If the canary appears, the file is being loaded.
- If the canary is missing, the file is not reaching Claude Code. Check the
  file location, the `@AGENTS.md` line in `CLAUDE.md`, and that you started
  Claude Code from the repository root.
- A canary shows that the file was **loaded**, not that every rule was
  **followed**. Check the plot code against each rule you wrote.

**You are done when** the canary appears in the code and the `CLAUDE.md` test
passes.

**If it goes wrong:** if the canary still does not appear after one restart,
switch to the `block5-done` branch from the Git pane's branch menu, which has a
working `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, and compare it with yours.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

Posit Assistant reads `AGENTS.md` directly as project memory, so it needs no
`CLAUDE.md`. Instead of copying the draft, you can have a short conversation
about your conventions and run `/savememory`. If the canary is missing, check
that you trusted the workspace.
:::

::::
:::


## Part B: Skills

A skill is a folder containing a `SKILL.md` file, and optionally scripts,
templates and reference files. Its `r glossary("front matter")`, the block
between two lines of three dashes at the top of `SKILL.md`, carries a `name`
and a `description`. Skills follow the open Agent Skills specification, so one
skill can serve several tools.

Two parts decide whether a skill works:

- **The description is the trigger.** The assistant reads descriptions to decide
  which skill is relevant. "Use when producing a ggplot2 figure for a report,
  poster or paper" loads when it should; "for plots" loads erratically.
  Invoking a skill by name (`/skill-name`) does not depend on the description.
- **The body is a procedure:** when to use the skill, the steps, hard rules, and
  a final check. Because a skill loads only when used, it can be longer than an
  instruction file.

For a skill that writes files or has other side effects, set
`disable-model-invocation: true` in the front matter, so it runs only when you
invoke it by name. Claude Code and Posit Assistant both support this field.


### Where skills live

| Location in the repository | Claude Code | Posit Assistant |
|---|---|---|
| `.agents/skills/<name>/` | — | Yes |
| `.claude/skills/<name>/` | Yes | — |
| `.posit/assistant/skills/<name>/` | — | Yes |

This course keeps the master copy of each skill in `.agents/skills/`, which
other tools also read, and **copies** the folder into `.claude/skills/` for
Claude Code. If you change a skill, copy it again. Copying from the R console
works the same on every system:

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
fs::dir_copy(
  here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"),
  here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)
```

On macOS or Linux you can use a `r glossary("symbolic link")` instead, so there
is only one copy: `fs::link_create(here::here(".agents", "skills",
"house-figures"), here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"))`. Claude
Code follows the link, but it stores the full path, so recreate it if you move
the project. On Windows, symbolic links need extra configuration, so copy the
folder.


### Activity: Write a skill and test it

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
A house figure style (20 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Start:** Claude Code running in `default` mode in your workshop project's
Terminal tab, with your `AGENTS.md` from the previous activity committed.

**1. Baseline, before the skill exists.** Ask:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_baseline.R.
```

Approve the edit when asked. Doing this first, before you create the skill,
guarantees the baseline was written without it, and the saved file gives the
later steps something to point at.

**2. Create the skill.** In the R console,
`usethis::edit_file(".agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md")` creates the
folder and the file and opens it. Paste in:

```markdown
---
name: house-figures
description: >-
  Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear
  in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a
  figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots.
---

# House figure style

## Rules
1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation
   (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar
   with error bars ("dynamite plot").
2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette
   (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same
   variable to point shape so the figure works without colour.
3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)".
4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12).
5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure.
6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a
   fitted model and asks for them.

## Before returning code
List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why.
```

Then copy the `house-figures` folder into `.claude/skills/`.

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
fs::dir_copy(
  here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"),
  here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)
```

**3. With the skill.** Leave Claude Code (`/exit`) and start it again with
`claude`, so it finds the new skill. Invoke the skill by name and ask the same
thing:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
/house-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles
data, for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_house.R.
```

**4. Grade it.** For each of the six rules, record whether the output complies:

| Rule | Without skill | With skill |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot | | |
| 2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape | | |
| 3. Units in axis titles | | |
| 4. `theme_classic(base_size = 12)` | | |
| 5. n per group shown | | |
| 6. No unrequested p-values | | |

Run both scripts in a fresh R session and look at the figures:
`callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "fig_baseline.R"))`, then the same for
`fig_house.R`. Code that names the right functions can still produce the
wrong picture.

**You are done when** the grading table is filled in from the figures you
looked at, not from the agent's list of rules it applied.

**If it goes wrong:** if the skill does not appear when you type `/`, check
that `.claude/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md` exists and restart Claude Code.
If you are out of time, switch to the `block5-done` branch from the Git pane's
branch menu.

**Payoff.** What did the skill do for you, how long did checking it take, and
would you use it again for the next figure?

**5. Test the trigger (optional, if time allows).** In a new Claude Code
conversation (`/clear`), without naming the skill, ask "Give me a quick look at
mass_post_g by arm" (exploratory, so the skill should *not* load). Then, in
another new conversation, ask "Polish the figure in scripts/fig_baseline.R for
the poster" (it *should* load). If either goes the wrong way, rewrite the
description and test again.

**6. Test a rule under pressure (optional).** Ask the assistant to "add
significance stars between the groups in scripts/fig_house.R". Rule 6 says it
should decline without a fitted model. Note whether it did. A skill is an
instruction, not a guarantee: what makes the output trustworthy is the grading
you did in step 4, which you can repeat on every figure.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

Posit Assistant reads `.agents/skills/` directly, so you do not need the copy in
`.claude/skills/`. Invoke the skill by name in the same way.
:::

::::
:::


### Skills you did not write

Each tool ships built-in skills. Claude Code bundles skills such as
`/code-review` and `/debug`. Collections of shared skills are published online,
for example Anthropic's `anthropics/skills` repository.

Before installing a skill someone else wrote, read it. A skill can include
scripts that the assistant may run on your machine, and its instructions shape
what the assistant does with your files and data. Treat it as you would any
code from the internet. *Going further* below gives you one to practise on:
`pub-figures`, the ggplot chapter's conventions packaged as a skill.


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **You can now:** state your conventions once and have every conversation
  follow them, and package a procedure as a skill you invoke by name,
  **trusted because** the canary and `tests/test_controls.R` show the files are
  connected, and you grade the output rule by rule.
- **Check:** the canary shows a file was loaded, not that its rules were
  followed; grade the output rule by rule, and run the figure code.
- **Reproduce:** your `AGENTS.md` now states the reproducibility rules (renv,
  fresh R session, seeds). They are requests; Blocks 7 and 9 check whether the
  agent kept to them.
- **Record:** add a line to `docs/ai-log.md` naming the skill you tested and
  what you changed in its output.
:::


## Check your understanding

**Your canary line does not appear in Claude Code's answers. What is the most
likely explanation?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Claude Code cannot follow instructions",
  answer = "The instructions are not reaching Claude Code, for example because CLAUDE.md does not import AGENTS.md or Claude Code was started outside the repository root",
  "The canary only works with Anthropic models",
  "AGENTS.md must be committed to GitHub before Claude Code can read it"
))`

**What is the essential difference between an instruction file and a skill?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Instruction files can contain code; skills cannot",
  answer = "Instructions load into every conversation automatically; a skill loads only when invoked by name or judged relevant from its description",
  "Skills are enforced; instructions are advisory",
  "Instruction files work only with Copilot"
))`

**A skill fires for quick exploratory plots when you meant it only for
publication figures. What should you change first?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The rules in the body of the skill",
  answer = "The description, so it states precisely when the skill applies and when it does not",
  "The folder the skill is stored in",
  "The model you are using"
))`


## Going further (not covered live)

This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if
it is useful to you.

### Instruction and skill files in other tools

| File or folder | Posit Assistant | GitHub Copilot |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` (repository root) | Read as project memory | Read by the cloud agent, agent mode and the CLI |
| `CLAUDE.md` | — | Read by the cloud agent |
| `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | Offered for conversion by `/import-instructions` | Read by Copilot |
| Path-scoped rules | No equivalent found | `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` with `applyTo` |
| `.agents/skills/<name>/` | Yes | Yes |
| `.claude/skills/<name>/` | — | Yes |
| `.github/skills/<name>/` | — | Yes |

Copilot's cloud agent reads both `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, so it may see the
conventions twice. That is harmless but wasteful, so keep `CLAUDE.md` to the
one import line. Copilot reads both `.agents/skills/` and `.claude/skills/`; if
it lists a skill twice, remove one route for Copilot.

Posit Assistant also includes built-in skills such as `quarto-authoring` and
`r-package-development`.

### A rule for Quarto files only

Some rules are right for one kind of file and wrong elsewhere. A chunk option
such as `#| echo: false` is meaningful in a `.qmd` file and meaningless in an
`.R` script. The test for a scoped rule: would it be *wrong*, not merely
irrelevant, in the files it excludes? If not, put it in `AGENTS.md`.

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Create and test a scoped rule
::::
::::{.task-container}

The rules themselves:

```markdown
# Quarto document conventions

- Set chunk options with the hashpipe (#|) inside the chunk, not in the
  {r} header.
- Give every chunk a label; prefix figure chunks with fig-.
- Every figure chunk sets #| fig-cap:, #| fig-width: and #| fig-height:.
- Refer to figures in the text with @fig-..., never by a typed number.
- Default to #| echo: false unless the document is a code walkthrough.
- Resolve paths with here::here(); never assume the working directory is the
  document's folder.
```

(The "hashpipe" is the `#|` at the start of a chunk-option line.) Place them
where your tool looks:

- **Claude Code:** `.claude/rules/quarto.md`, beginning with front matter that
  restricts it to Quarto files:

  ```text
  ---
  paths:
    - "**/*.qmd"
  ---
  ```

- **Copilot:** `.github/instructions/quarto.instructions.md`, beginning with
  this front matter:

  ```text
  ---
  applyTo: "**/*.qmd"
  ---
  ```

- **Posit Assistant:** no path-scoped instruction file is documented. Add the
  rules to `AGENTS.md` under a heading such as "When editing .qmd files", or
  rely on its built-in `quarto-authoring` skill.

**Test.** Open a `.qmd` file and ask for a chunk that plots `mass_post_g` by
`treatment_arm`. A correct answer uses hashpipe options, a `fig-` label, a
caption and `here::here()`. Then ask for the same plot in an `.R` script; the
Quarto rules should not appear. If they do not appear in the `.qmd` either, the
rule is not loading on your surface. Report what you found; behaviour differs
between tools.

::::
:::

Every scoped rule is a second copy of a convention to keep in step, once per
tool. Use scoped rules sparingly.

### Install a skill bundle and compare

`house-figures` is six rules you wrote and can read at a glance. `pub-figures`
is the opposite case: the conventions from the ggplot chapter (the chart-type
and audience tables, `theme_project()`, colorspace palettes, the
colour-vision-deficiency check, the four-element legend, saving in two
formats) packaged as a skill of about 200 lines, with R scripts that the
assistant sources and adapts. It is a skill you did not write, so you read it
before you install it.

The bundle contains:

```text
pub-figures/
├── SKILL.md                when to use it, the rules, a pre-flight checklist
├── theme-project.R         theme_project() and palette functions
├── raincloud-template.R    figure skeleton, including saving
├── emmeans-bridge.R        model-based significance brackets
└── patchwork-template.R    multi-panel figure with one shared legend
```

`theme_project()` in this bundle is the full version of the simple
`theme_project()` you wrote in the ggplot chapter: the same name and
`base_size` argument, with a font, colours for titles and gridlines, and an
`axis_type` argument added.

```{r}
#| echo: false
skill_download_button("pub-figures")
```

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
A skill bundle you did not write
::::
::::{.task-container}

**1. Read before you install.** Open `SKILL.md` and `theme-project.R` (both are
also reproduced below). Find two places where `pub-figures` contradicts your
`house-figures` rules. (There are at least two: the palette and the theme.)
Find the line that tells the assistant what to do when information is
missing.

**2. Remove the overlap.** Both skills describe themselves as being for
figures in reports, posters and papers, so with both installed you cannot tell
which one loaded. Move `house-figures` out of both skills folders (or rename
`SKILL.md` inside it) before going on. Overlapping descriptions are a real
hazard once you collect skills from several sources.

**3. Install.** In the R console,
`unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills"))` lets you pick
the downloaded zip and unpacks it into `.agents/skills/`; then copy it into
`.claude/skills/` for Claude Code with `fs::dir_copy()`, as above. The skill uses ggdist,
colorspace, ragg, colorBlindness, emmeans and ggpubr; if your project uses
renv and they are not in its lockfile, add them yourself before the test,
rather than letting the assistant install packages.

**4. Same prompt, new skill.** Restart Claude Code so it finds the skill, then,
without naming the skill, ask the prompt from the house-figures activity:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report.
```

Did the skill load from its description alone? Did the assistant ask about
the audience, or record a default?

**5. Grade it against its own checklist.** The skill ends with a pre-flight
checklist. Check the script against each item yourself, rather than accepting
the assistant's report that it did. Then run the script: are both a PDF and a
PNG in `outputs/figures/`? Run the `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` line it left
for you, and look at the result.

**6. Test a rule under pressure.** Ask it to "add significance stars between
the groups" without fitting a model. The skill says it must insert a legend
placeholder rather than invent p-values. Then give it a fitted model it can
actually see. Claude Code cannot see objects in your R console, so a model you
fit there does not count: ask it to add
`model <- lm(mass_post_g ~ treatment_arm, data = voles)` to the figure script
itself, or paste the output of `summary(model)` into the prompt. Ask again: it
should now use the `emmeans-bridge.R` pattern with an adjusted p-value.

**7. Compare.** Which skill would you hand to a colleague? Which would you
trust without rereading it after an update? A long skill encodes more of your
standards, and hides more of them from view.
